title: Erasure coding for six validators: three octets into six chunks, and back
summary: The data $\mathbf{d}$, 3 octets, is padded with zeroes to a multiple of $2\mathcal{D}(v)$ = 6 octets, so it is one word (two octets) for each of 3 runs. The code $\mathcal{C}^6_1$ is systematic: the first 3 chunks are the data itself, and the other 3 are parity. Any 3 chunks give the data back.

rows.label: Chunk 0 (validator 0)
cells: data: octets 0–1 of the padded data

rows.label: Chunk 1 (validator 1)
cells: data: octets 2–3 of the padded data

rows.label: Chunk 2 (validator 2)
cells: data: octets 4–5 of the padded data

params: $v$ = 6 validators, so $\mathcal{D}(v)$ = 3: any 3 of the 6 chunks recover the data
notes: Each chunk is one word because the padded data is one word per run ($k$ = 1). Longer data gives each chunk one word per piece, with the same code applied to every piece.
The first recovery uses only parity chunks, so the model interpolates through the field of §H.2; the second mixes data and parity.
name: erasure-tiny
check: The model's six chunks equal the vector's shards (the comparison `lake build erasuretest` makes on every erasure vector), and recovering from each subset above gives the padded data back.
